quote: Beweise dass die Gleichung $x^n + \binom{n}{1}^\alpha x^{n-1} + \binom{n}{2}^\alpha x^{n-2} + \dots + 1 = 0$ für $\alpha > 1$ lauter reelle, für $\alpha < 1$ lauter [-kleine-] imaginäre Wurzeln hat. ausser einer für ungerades $n$.
english: Prove that the equation x^n + (n choose 1)^alpha x^{n-1} + (n choose 2)^alpha x^{n-2} + ... + 1 = 0 has only real roots for alpha > 1, and only imaginary roots for alpha < 1, except for one when n is odd.
topic: Two exercises: proving that a polynomial with binomial coefficients raised to a power alpha has all real roots for alpha > 1 and all imaginary roots for alpha < 1, and a plan to prove the irrationality/transcendence of e and pi without integrals by replacing the integral with the limit of a sum.

triage.modern_statement: For real α and integer n ≥ 1, let P_{n,α}(x) = Σ_{k=0}^{n} C(n,k)^α x^k. This is a self-reciprocal polynomial with positive coefficients, so any real root it has is negative. Hilbert's claim has two parts. (a) For α > 1, every root of P_{n,α} is real. (b) For α < 1, every root is non-real, except the root x = −1 that is forced when n is odd. α = 1 is the boundary case: (x+1)^n has the single root −1 repeated n times, and α = 0 gives 1 + x + … + x^n, whose roots lie on the unit circle. So the question asks whether α = 1 is the exact threshold between real-rootedness and having no real roots for these 'powered binomial' polynomials.
triage.answered_by: My searches found no source that answers, cites or discusses this question. My own check suggests that part (a), as written, is false. Take n = 4 and substitute y = x + 1/x. This gives y^2 + 4^α y + (6^α − 2) = 0. All four x-roots are real only if both y-roots are real and have |y| ≥ 2. Write α = 1 + ε with ε small and positive. The y-roots are real, but the larger one is about −2 + 0.58·√ε, which lies above −2. So P_{4,1+ε} has two non-real roots. High-precision numerical root-finding (mpmath, 60 digits) agrees. For α = 1.01, n = 4, 6, 8 and 10 each have only 2 real roots. For α = 1.2, n = 4 is fully real-rooted but n = 6, 8 and 10 are not. For α = 1.5, every n I tested (up to 15) was real-rooted. So real-rootedness for α > 1 appears to need α to be large enough, depending on n; it does not start right at α = 1. From memory and without a source in hand: for integer α ≥ 2, real-rootedness should follow from the classical Maló–Schur results on Hadamard (coefficient-wise) products of real-rooted polynomials. Part (b) held in every case I tested (α = 0.3, 0.9, 0.99 with n from 2 to 15: no real roots except −1 for odd n). I found no published proof of it.
triage.why: The question is precise, but none of my searches turned up a paper that addresses it, and the search tool's quota ran out before I could try more specific queries (Pólya–Szegő exercises, Maló/Schur composition theorems, the history of Hilbert's notes). The only results I got were about other families of binomial-type polynomials, so I have listed no sources as evidence. It is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem. My computations, not any source, show that part (a) fails as stated for α slightly above 1 (n = 4 can be checked by hand). That may be why Hilbert left it open. Part (b) looks numerically true but I did not find a proof. Real-rootedness of coefficient-transformed polynomials (multiplier sequences, Hadamard products) is a live research area in general. I cannot confirm that this particular question has been studied.
